blocks.raw:
<LawCallout code="pd1096" section="Rule I - Building Permits">


The 15-day clock begins at payment — not submission — because compliance review before payment can take days or weeks as the applicant corrects deficiencies. Once fees are paid, the application is deemed complete and the OBO is legally obligated to act. This protects the applicant from indefinite bureaucratic delay.


</LawCallout>

blocks.raw: Reveal Answer **Correct Answer: B** **Analysis:** - The **tool shed** (5 sq.m., detached, private use) is a "minor construction" under Sec. 301.3.a.i of the Revised IRR — sheds not exceeding 6.00 sq.m., completely detached, private use. It is **exempt from the building permit itself**. - The **bamboo house** (native materials, family use, P12,000 — under P15,000) qualifies as a "traditional indigenous family dwelling" under Sec. 209, PD 1096. It **requires a building permit** but is **exempt from paying fees**. - Option A is wrong: the tool shed does not merely skip fees — it skips the permit entirely. - Option C reverses the two exemptions. - Option D is wrong: the bamboo house still needs a permit. **Rule to lock in:** Fee exemption (Sec. 209) ≠ Permit exemption (Sec. 301.3, IRR). They are different lists with different criteria.

blocks.raw: Reveal Answer **Correct Answer: B — March 16** **Analysis:** Under Sec. 304 of PD 1096, the Building Official must issue or deny the permit within **15 days from payment of the required fees**. Payment occurred on March 1, so the deadline is March 16. - Option A (February 25) would apply if the clock started at submission — it does not. - Option C (March 31) is 30 days from payment — no basis in law. - Option D has no legal support; the BO is on a hard 15-day statutory deadline. If denied, the BO must communicate the denial **in writing within the same 15-day period**, specifying which Code provisions were not met.

blocks.raw: Reveal Answer **Correct Answer: D — 100% of building permit fees** **Analysis:** The surcharge table under Sec. 212 of the Revised IRR is: - Excavation: 10% - Foundation: 25% - Superstructure up to 2.00 m: 50% - Superstructure **above 2.00 m**: **100%** At 3.0 m above grade, the structure is in the top bracket — the maximum 100% surcharge applies. The owner must pay the building permit fees **plus** an additional amount equal to 100% of those fees as a penalty surcharge.

blocks.raw: Reveal Answer **Correct Answer: C — Accessory Permit required** **Analysis:** The fence rules under the Revised IRR have three distinct thresholds: - Garden masonry walls **1.20 m and below**: fully exempt from any permit (Sec. 301.3.a.v) - Fences **above 1.20 m up to 1.80 m**: **Accessory Permit required** (Sec. 301.2.b.ii) - Fences **above 1.80 m**: Full Building Permit required as Group J-2 occupancy (Sec. 701, IRR) A 1.60 m fence falls in the middle bracket — Accessory Permit only. Option A is the most common wrong answer because many candidates believe 1.80 m is the lower threshold. It is actually the upper threshold for the Accessory Permit bracket.

blocks.raw: Reveal Answer **Correct Answer: A — January 15 of the following year** **Analysis:** Under Sec. 305 of PD 1096, a building permit becomes null and void if construction has **not commenced within one (1) year** from the date of issue. Issued January 15 → expires January 15 of the following year if no work has started. The 120-day rule (Option B) applies to **abandonment** — once construction has started, a continuous 120-day stoppage voids the permit. These are two separate triggers, and the exam will often test whether you can distinguish them.
